'''Stuart Lawrence Licht''' is an American chemist and academic. He is a Professor Emeritus of Chemistry at [[George Washington University]] (GWU). Licht's research focuses on carbon capture to mitigate climate change and the electrochemical conversion of carbon dioxide into nanocarbons and other useful society stables, as well as solar energy, battery chemistry, and physical/analytical chemistry.

His earlier works primarily focused on fundamental physical and analytical chemistry, high efficiency solar cells, and photo-electrochemistry.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" ==Early life and education==
Licht was born in Boston, Massachusetts. He earned a [[Bachelor of Science]] degree in 1976 and a [[Master of Science]] in 1980 from [[Wesleyan University]], where he conducted research in molecular [[quantum mechanics]]. He completed his Ph.D. in 1985 at the [[Weizmann Institute of Science]] in materials chemistry, with a focus on photoelectrochemical solar cells.<ref name="TheConversation">{{cite web |title=Stuart Licht |url=https://theconversation.com/profiles/stuart-licht-134155 |website=The Conversation |date=7 August 2014}}</ref> From 1986 to 1988, he was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT), where he studied, developed theory on, and experimented with microelectrode and chemical diffusion under the guidance of  [[Mark S. Wrighton]].<ref name=":8" /><ref name=":12">{{cite journal | last1=Wrighton | first1=Mark S. | last2=Licht | first2=Stuart | title=Microelectrodes and Their Use in Photochemistry and Electrochemistry | journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society | volume=112 | issue=12 | pages=4677–4682 | year=1988 | doi=10.1021/ja00167a010}}</ref>

==Academic career==
From 1988 to 1995, Licht held the Carlson Endowed Chair in Chemistry at [[Clark University]]. He subsequently served at the [[Technion – Israel Institute of Technology]] from 1995 to 2003,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Radin |first1=Rick |title=Technion team helping to make hydrogen fuel cells work in cars |url=https://www.israel21c.org/technion-team-helping-to-make-hydrogen-fuel-cells-work-in-cars/ |website=Israel21c |access-date=15 May 2025 |date=28 October 2002}}</ref> and then chaired the Department of Chemistry at the [[University of Massachusetts]] from 2003 to 2008.<ref>{{cite web |title=Stuart Licht: "Powering Tomorrow Towards a Sustainable Energy Future" |url=https://energy.umd.edu/news/story/stuart-licht-powering-tomorrow-towards-a-sustainable-energy-future |website=Umd.edu |access-date=15 May 2025}}</ref> He also worked as a Program Director at the [[National Science Foundation]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Researcher Nabs $1.7 Million to Study 'Solar Cement' {{!}} GW Today {{!}} The George Washington University |url=https://gwtoday.gwu.edu/researcher-nabs-17-million-study-solar-cement |website=GW Today |access-date=15 May 2025}}</ref> In 2008, he joined [[George Washington University]], where he became Professor Emeritus of Chemistry in 2023.<ref>{{cite web |title=Licht, Stuart {{!}} Department of Chemistry {{!}} Columbian College of Arts & Sciences |url=https://chemistry.columbian.gwu.edu/stuart-licht |website=George Washington University |language=en}}</ref>

He has chaired the New England Section of the [[American Chemical Society]] and is a Fellow of the [[Electrochemical Society]],<ref>{{cite web |title=Fellow of The Electrochemical Society |url=https://www.electrochem.org/fellow |website=ECS |access-date=15 May 2025}}</ref> where he founded both the New England and Israel sections.

==Research==
Licht's research is centered on developing carbon-negative technologies. His work on liquid solar solar cells pursued (1) discovery of the role of solution chemistry in the mechanism and enhancement of photoelectrochemical (semiconductors immersed in electrolytes) solar energy conversion,<ref name=":3" /> (2) development of a solar cell with built energy charge storage,<ref name=":4" /> (3) multi-bandgap photoelectrochemistry,<ref>{{Cite book |title=Encyclopedia of electrochemistry |date=2002 |publisher=Wiley-VCH |isbn=978-3-527-30250-5 |editor-last=Bard |editor-first=Allen J. |location=Weinheim}}</ref> (4) a light addressable sensor<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Licht |first1=Stuart |last2=Myung |first2=Noseung |last3=Sun |first3=Yue |date=1996-01-01 |title=A Light Addressable Photoelectrochemical Cyanide Sensor |journal=Analytical Chemistry |volume=68 |issue=6 |pages=954–959 |doi=10.1021/ac9507449 |bibcode=1996AnaCh..68..954L |issn=0003-2700}}</ref> and (5) highest solar conversion efficiencies for solar water splitting to produce hydrogen.<ref name=":20">{{Cite journal |last1=Licht |first1=Stuart |last2=Wang |first2=Bahoui |last3=Mukerji |first3=Sudeshna |last4=Soga |first4 = Tetsuo | last5 = Umeno | first5 = Masayoshi | last6=Tributsh | first6 = Helmuth |date=July 2001 |title=Over 18% solar energy conversion to generation of hydrogen fuel; theory and experiment for efficient solar water splitting |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0360319900001336 |journal=International Journal of Hydrogen Energy |volume=26 |issue=7 |pages=653–659 |bibcode=2001IJHE...26..653L |doi=10.1016/S0360-3199(00)00133-6 |url-access=subscription}}</ref>
[[File:StrontiumC2CNTPlant.jpg|thumb|CO<sub>2</sub> emitted from the Shepard 860 MW NG Power plant in Calgary, CA, using Stuart Licht Technology at his company, is directly converted to carbon nanotubes or carbon nano-onions at high purity by tuning the electrochemical conditions of the C2CNT process using the Genesis Device Modules. Both pure lithium carbonate and strontium/lithium carbonate was used in this technology, with mixed electrolyte being much cheaper and developed later on.<ref name=":42">{{Cite journal |last1=Hofstetter |first1=Kyle |last2=Licht |first2=Gad |last3=Licht |first3=Stuart |date=2025-09-01 |title=Comparative Analysis of Amine, Lime, and Molten Carbonate Electrolytic CO 2 Carbon Capture |journal=ECS Advances |volume=4 |issue=3 |page=031002 |doi=10.1149/2754-2734/adf56a |issn=2754-2734|doi-access=free }}</ref>]]
[[File:Stuart Licht ACS Conference CO2 to CNM.jpg|thumb|Stuart Licht's ACS Conference on CO2 to CNM (2015).]]

carbon nanomaterials.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Licht |first1=S |last2=Wang |first2=B |last3=Mukerji |first3=S |last4=Soga |first4=T |last5=Umeno |first5=M |last6=Tributsch |first6=H |date=2001-07-01 Scale-up during this time included developing novel pressing based extraction method to extract carbon nanomaterials from electrolyte at high pressures.<ref name=":34">{{Cite journal |last1=Hofstetter |first1=Kyle |last2=Licht |first2=Gad |last3=Licht |first3=Stuart |date=2025-09-01 |title=Industrial scaling of molten carbonate electrolytic carbon capture and production of graphene allotropes |journal=DeCarbon |volume=9 |article-number=100122 |doi=10.1016/j.decarb.2025.100122 |issn=2949-8813|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Later on, he investigated C2CNT's CNT to create a unique, cold dusty plasma through microwave radiation efficiently shown below as an image and video.<ref name=":43">{{Cite journal |last1=Licht |first1=Gad |last2=Hofstetter |first2=Kyle |last3=Licht |first3=Stuart |date=2025-04-10 |title=Intense, self-induced sustainable microwave plasma using carbon nanotubes made from CO2 |journal=Nanoscale |language=en |volume=17 |issue=15 |pages=9279–9296 |doi=10.1039/D4NR04097J |issn=2040-3372|doi-access=free |pmid=39883035 }}</ref>
[[File:Microwave induced dusty plasma generated by C2CNT CNTs.jpg|thumb|Microwave induced plasma created by C2CNT's CNTs hot enough to melt a flask.<ref name=":43" />]]
[[File:Microwave generating plasma catalyzed by C2CNT CNTs.webm|thumb|Microwave generating plasma catalyzed by C2CNT CNTs. Hot enough to melt glass beakers.<ref name="ReferenceA"/>]]

Licht is the grandson of industrial chemist Joseph Licht, published with his father analytical chemist Truman Licht, and published and patent extensively with his son Gad Licht. His over 900 patents and publications, have often focused on removal of the greenhouse gases.<ref name=":29" /><ref name=":31">{{Cite web |title=Stuart LICHT {{!}} George Washington University, D.C. {{!}} GW {{!}} Department of Chemistry {{!}} Research profile |url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Stuart-Licht |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230219024303/https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Stuart-Licht |archive-date=2023-02-19 |access-date=2025-11-26 |website=ResearchGate |language=en}}</ref> He also has an extensive presence in the journals ''Nature'' and ''Science.''<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /><ref name=":6" /><ref name=":7" /><ref name=":8" /><ref name=":9" /><ref name=":10" /><ref name=":11" /><ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name="TheConversation" /><ref name=":12" />
